Arjuna. One of the five Pandava princes and a central hero of the Mahabharata, the world's longest epic poem.

Arjuna is a warrior of extraordinary skill and virtue, best remembered as the recipient of Krishna's philosophical teachings in the Bhagavad Gita. This sacred dialogue forms the ethical and spiritual cornerstone of Hindu philosophy.

Arjuna is one of the five Pandava brothers, legitimate heirs to the throne whose right to rule is contested in the great war of Kurukshetra. He is an unparalleled archer and master of martial arts, blessed with divine weapons and the favor of the gods themselves.

On the eve of battle, Arjuna struggles with moral doubt. He questions the righteousness of fighting his own cousins and kinsmen. This existential crisis is resolved when Krishna appears as his charioteer and delivers the Bhagavad Gita, a transformative philosophical discourse that addresses his deepest concerns about duty, action, and righteousness.

Arjuna is married to Draupadi. Her public humiliation at the gambling table becomes a pivotal cause of the great conflict. He journeys through exile and hardship alongside his brothers, embodying resilience and devotion to dharma despite profound suffering.

He carries Gandiva, a divine bow gifted by the fire god Agni, making him the most feared archer of his age. His dialogue with Krishna establishes the path of karma yoga, disciplined action without attachment to results. This principle remains central to Hindu ethics and spiritual philosophy.

Through his struggle with moral doubt and his ultimate acceptance of his duty, Arjuna becomes the model for the seeker who must act righteously even when uncertain of the outcome.
